paragraphs: The first sound Andrew Walker heard that morning was someone singing in the corridor.

It was a terrible song. Not because the singer lacked enthusiasm. There was far too much enthusiasm for six in the morning, and whoever had invented the tune hadn't bothered with the inconvenience of a melody.
Andrew opened one eye.
Across the little room, Nicolas Vallée lay faceup on his bunk with a pillow pressed over his head. One hand emerged long enough to give the ceiling an offended gesture.
“Tell him,” Nico said through the pillow.
“Tell him what?”
“That his kitchen is on the other side of the building.”
The singing continued, followed by a metallic crash and a very recognizable voice saying, “I'm all right.”
Andrew pulled his blanket higher. “I think he's figured that out.”
“He hasn't. He's singing again.”

The room had been an office before the war. There was still a painted rectangle on the wall where a noticeboard had hung, and the two beds had to be arranged foot-to-foot because there wasn't room to put them any other way. Someone had screwed a narrow shelf above Andrew's pillow. It held a torch, two paperback books, and a clock whose green numerals insisted that it was 06:14.
He was nineteen. He had been in charge of their outpost for almost four months. Neither fact had made mornings any easier.
From outside came three impatient knocks.
“Andrew?” Darius called. “Are you awake?”
“No,” Andrew said.
“Good. I need a second opinion.”
“On what?”
“Something I made.”
Nico removed the pillow. His dark curls stuck up on one side. “Tell him you're dead.”
“Then he'll make enough for seven.”
“That would be a kindness.”

Andrew sat up. His uniform trousers hung from the end of the bed; his boots stood underneath them, close enough to reach without stepping on the cold floor. The heater had gone off again in the night. The military could provide eight trained mech pilots and a building full of expensive equipment, but it apparently couldn't maintain a radiator.
He pulled on his socks and opened the door.

Darius Okafor filled most of the passage. He was wearing an apron over his base clothes and holding a spoon with a smear of something pale and thick on it. Behind him, the converted depot stretched away in a line of old offices. The windows were wet with rain. A yellow emergency lamp burned at the far end of the hall, illuminating a sign that read CONSERVE POWER in three languages.
Darius offered the spoon.
Andrew stared at it. “What is it?”
“Breakfast.”
“That's not an answer.”
“It's supposed to be porridge.”
“Supposed to be?”
“I'd like an unbiased assessment before I tell you what went into it.”
Andrew considered the spoon. Darius was tall enough that Andrew had to look up slightly, and his expression was so hopeful that refusing felt worse than whatever was in the bowl.
He tasted it.
For a moment he could identify oats. Then came cinnamon, something sour, and a flavor that he had no intention of guessing.
Darius watched his face.
“That's interesting,” Andrew said.
“Interesting good?”
“Interesting in a historical sense. People will talk about it.”
From behind Andrew, Nico called, “Ask him whether it can strip paint.”
Darius leaned around the doorframe. “I heard that.”
“You were meant to,” Nico said.
Darius took back the spoon, looking more thoughtful than insulted. “I used the powdered milk.”
“Did you check the label?” Andrew asked.
“Of course.”
“Both sides?”
Darius glanced down at his spoon.
Andrew knew that look. It was the same expression people wore when they remembered an exam question two minutes after handing in the paper.
“Breakfast at seven,” Darius said, and departed at speed.
Nico swung his legs off the bed. “He'll be fine. He still has forty minutes to invent a new one.”
“He had forty minutes,” Andrew said. “Now he has thirty-six.”
He shut the door before Nico could throw the pillow.

By the time Andrew reached the washroom, the building had begun waking around him. Pipes clicked in the walls. Someone had turned on the radio in the common room. Through the washroom's steamed-up window he could see the hangar beyond the courtyard, a long concrete structure with two wide doors and rainwater gathering in the cracks of the apron.
Eight XR-17s lived there, if lived was the word for machines that required more attention than the people operating them.

Their base had once been a municipal maintenance depot. Now concrete barriers divided the vehicle yard, cables ran along the outer walls, and a pair of watch posts looked east across empty fields. Beyond those fields lay the routes the Reclaimed used when they pressed against the remaining defenses. Beyond the defenses, to the west, were the towns and crowded cities that humanity still held.
The rest of the world was gone to them. Germany was where the survivors had gathered, and the XR-17s were one of the reasons a refuge still existed at all.
Andrew brushed his teeth, rinsed the sink, and decided that those facts were easier to contemplate after breakfast.
When he entered the common room, Akari Sato was taking a photograph of an empty chair.
She stood with her camera raised, long black ponytail hanging over the shoulder of a faded sweatshirt. She moved sideways, frowned at the display, and tried again.
Andrew looked from her to the chair. “Did it do something worth remembering?”
“I'm testing the light.”
“On a chair?”
“It's a very patient subject.”
“Unlike the rest of us?”
Akari lowered the camera. “Exactly. Also, don't make plans for this afternoon.”
“I already have plans.”
“Cancel them.”
“My plans include ensuring the machines that keep us alive continue doing so.”
“Good. Then you'll already be at the hangar.”
Andrew stopped reaching for the coffee tin. “Akari.”
“Group picture,” she said. “Outside. In front of the mechs. Everybody.”
“We have pictures.”
“We have old pictures.”
“Photographs generally work that way.”
Akari gave him the smile she used when she had decided an argument was already over. “Four o'clock. If the rain stops.”
Andrew found the coffee tin empty.
“Do I get a vote?” he asked.
“You can vote on where to stand.”
He turned the tin upside down anyway. A few grains fell into his palm.
Akari watched him with genuine sympathy. “That's heartbreaking.”
“Are you going to photograph this too?”
“Only if you cry.”

The doorway opened again. Mara Venn entered carrying a waterproof map case under one arm. Her long chestnut hair was tied back, and her boots had brought half the courtyard with her. She looked at the empty coffee tin in Andrew's hand and set a small, still-sealed packet beside it.
“From the watch post,” Mara said. “They owed me.”
Andrew lifted it reverently. “I'm putting you in charge of morale.”
“No, thank you. That's your problem.”

Mara had been outside checking the eastern access road before most of the building stirred. She had made a note of the morning's rainfall on the route sheet and had her usual list of things to complain about, which meant she was in a good mood by Mara's standards.
“Tomorrow's patrol,” she said, tapping the map case. “We need to talk before Juno takes his machine out.”
“Something wrong with the route?”
“Something wrong with half the route.”
Akari pointed her camera at them.
“Not now,” Andrew and Mara said together.
Akari took the picture anyway.
